example.pinyin: Tā wǔrǔ le wǒ de péngyou.
example.english: He insulted my friend.
example.fact: 侮 rarely appears alone in modern Mandarin — it mainly shows up in the compound 侮辱 (wǔrǔ), meaning 'to insult.'

components.note: 艹 (grass) — 藩's oldest meaning was a fence woven from plant stalks, so the grass root anchors that image.
潘 (Pān) gives a sound related to fān, sharing the final -an though the initial consonant has drifted apart over time.

example.english: The fence is very tall.
example.fact: 藩 rarely appears alone in modern Mandarin — it mainly survives in the word 藩篱 (fánlí), meaning 'fence' or 'barrier.'

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 拂 describes a hand brushing or flicking something away.
弗 (fú) gives the sound — an exact match with 拂.

example.english: The spring breeze gently brushes the face.
example.fact: 拂 often pairs with 风 in phrases like 春风拂面 (chūnfēng fú miàn), 'the spring breeze brushes one's face,' a common poetic image in Chinese.

components.note: 鸟 (bird) — 鹤 names a type of bird, the crane.
隺 (hú) gives a sound distantly related to hè, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: The crane is a symbol of longevity.
example.fact: In Chinese culture, the crane (鹤) is a traditional symbol of longevity and is often paired with pine trees in art.

etymologyHint: An insect 虫 bite 饣; 饣 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 饣 depicts food or something edible.
虫 depicts an insect — paired with food, the image is of something small nibbling away at it, giving 蚀 its meaning 'to erode, to eat into.'

example.english: There is a solar eclipse today.
example.fact: 蚀 most often appears in 腐蚀 (fǔshí, 'to corrode') and 日蚀 (rìshí, 'solar eclipse').

components.note: 水 (water) — 浆 describes a thick liquid, like starch mixed with water.
丬 (qiáng) gives a sound close to jiāng, sharing a similar final.

example.english: I drink soy milk for breakfast.
example.fact: 浆 is best known from 豆浆 (dòujiāng), soy milk, a classic Chinese breakfast drink.

meanings: used in 芙蓉[fu2 rong2], lotus

components.note: 艹 (flower/plant) — 芙 names a flowering plant.
夫 (fū) gives a sound close to fú, sharing the same initial and vowel, differing only in tone.

example.english: Hibiscus flowers are very beautiful.
example.fact: 芙 never appears alone — it only exists in the word 芙蓉 (fúróng), referring to the hibiscus or lotus flower.

components.note: 土 (earth) — 垃 relates to piled-up waste or debris on the ground.
立 (lì) gives a sound distantly related to lā, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: There is trash in the trash can.
example.fact: 垃 never stands alone — it only appears in 垃圾 (lājī), the everyday word for 'garbage' or 'trash.'

meanings: to warm oneself by a fire

components.note: 火 (fire) — 烤 describes cooking directly over fire or heat.
考 (kǎo) gives the sound — an exact match with 烤.

example.english: Beijing roast duck is very famous.
example.fact: 烤 is the character behind 烤鸭 (kǎoyā), Beijing's world-famous roast duck dish.

meanings: to dry (clothes, grain etc) in the sun

components.note: 日 (sun) — 晒 describes something exposed to sunlight.
西 (xī) gives a sound distantly related to shài, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: Cats like to bask in the sun.
example.fact: 晒 is the verb used in 晒太阳 (shài tàiyáng), literally 'to sun the sun,' meaning 'to bask in sunlight.'

meanings: white powder or cream spread over a surface

components.note: 雨 (rain) — 霜 belongs to the same family of weather characters as rain and snow.
相 (xiāng) gives a sound close to shuāng, sharing a similar rhyme.

example.english: There was frost on the grass this morning.
example.fact: 霜 (frost) forms on cold, clear nights when water vapor freezes directly onto surfaces like grass.

components.note: 刂 (knife) — 剿 describes wiping out an enemy by force.
巢 (cháo) gives a sound distantly related to jiǎo, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: The army wiped out the bandits.
example.fact: 剿 is a formal, military word mainly seen in 剿灭 (jiǎomiè) or 围剿 (wéijiǎo), both meaning 'to wipe out' or 'suppress' by force.

components.note: 艹 (plant) — 蕴's original sense was of plants accumulating and growing thick, extended to mean 'to store up.'
缊 (yūn) gives a sound close to yùn, the same syllable with a different tone.

example.english: This story contains a lesson.
example.fact: 蕴 usually appears in 蕴含 (yùnhán), meaning 'to contain' or 'to imply,' often used for stories or words with a deeper meaning.

components.note: 土 (earth) — 圾 relates to loose earth or debris; it survives only as half of a compound word.
及 (jí) gives a sound close to jī, the same syllable with a different tone.

example.english: There is trash everywhere on the ground.
example.fact: 圾 only exists as the second half of 垃圾 (lājī), 'garbage' — it has no independent meaning or use.

components.note: 纟 (silk) — 绸 names a type of woven silk fabric.
周 (zhōu) gives a sound close to chóu, sharing the same final and both retroflex initials.

example.english: Chinese silk is very famous.
example.fact: 绸 is part of 丝绸 (sīchóu), 'silk,' the fabric that gave the ancient Silk Road (丝绸之路) its name.

components.note: 山 (mountain) — 屿 refers to a small landform surrounded by water.
与 (yǔ) gives the sound — an exact match with 屿.

example.english: This island is very small.
example.fact: 屿 rarely stands alone — it almost always pairs with 岛 as 岛屿 (dǎoyǔ), the general word for 'island.'

components.note: 气 (gas) — 氢 names one of the lightest gases, hydrogen.
工 (gōng) gives a sound distantly related to qīng, having drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Qīng shì zuì qīng de yuánsù.
example.english: Hydrogen is the lightest element.
example.fact: 氢 (hydrogen) is the lightest and most abundant element in the universe.

components.note: 马 (horse) — 驼 groups the camel with other animals like the horse.
它 (tā) gives a sound distantly related to tuó, sharing the initial t- but with a rhyme that has since drifted.

example.english: Camels live in the desert.
example.fact: 驼 only appears in 骆驼 (luòtuo), 'camel' — animals famous for surviving long journeys through the desert without water.

components.note: 女 (woman) — 妆 describes putting on makeup, an action tied to appearance.
丬 gives a sound related to zhuāng, though the connection has drifted apart over time.

example.english: She puts on makeup every day.
example.fact: 妆 is the character in 化妆 (huàzhuāng), 'to put on makeup,' and 化妆品 (huàzhuāngpǐn), 'cosmetics.'

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 捆 describes the action of tying something with the hands.
困 (kùn) gives a sound close to kǔn, the same syllable with a different tone.

example.pinyin: Zhèxiē bàozhǐ kǔn de hěn jǐn.
example.english: These newspapers are tied up very tightly.
example.fact: 捆 is a common verb for tying things into a bundle, and also works as a measure word — 一捆 (yī kǔn) means 'a bundle of' something.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 铅 names a metal, lead.
几 (jī) gives a sound distantly related to qiān, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: I write with a pencil.
example.fact: 铅 (lead) gives 铅笔 (qiānbǐ, 'pencil') its name, even though pencil 'leads' are actually made of graphite, not the metal lead.

components.note: 辶 (walk) — 逛 describes moving around, like strolling.
狂 (kuáng) gives a sound close to guàng, sharing the same rhyme.

example.english: We go window-shopping on weekends.
example.fact: 逛 is best known from 逛街 (guàngjiē), the everyday phrase for strolling around shops and streets, whether or not you actually buy anything.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 淑's original sense was 'clear, pure water,' later extended to describe a person's pure character.
叔 (shū) gives the sound — an exact match with 淑.

example.english: She is a refined lady.
example.fact: 淑 today survives mainly in 淑女 (shūnǚ), a somewhat old-fashioned word for a gentle, well-mannered woman.

components.note: 木 (tree) — 榴 names a fruit that grows on a tree.
留 (liú) gives the sound — an exact match with 榴.

example.english: Pomegranates taste a bit sour.
example.fact: 榴 never appears alone — it only exists in words like 石榴 (shíliú, 'pomegranate') and 榴莲 (liúlián, 'durian').

example.english: Option C is the correct answer.
example.fact: 丙 is the third of the traditional 'heavenly stems,' often used like the letter 'C' to label a third item in a list.

components.note: 疒 (sickness) — 痒 belongs to the group of characters describing bodily discomfort.
羊 (yáng) gives a sound close to yǎng, the same syllable with a different tone.

example.english: My hand is very itchy.
example.fact: 痒 is the everyday word for the sensation of itchiness.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 钞 groups paper currency with other value-related characters marked by the metal radical.
少 (shǎo) gives a sound close to chāo, sharing a similar rhyme.

example.pinyin: Tā qiánbāo lǐ yǒu hěn duō chāopiào.
example.english: He has a lot of banknotes in his wallet.
example.fact: 钞 mainly appears in 钞票 (chāopiào), the everyday word for paper money, 'banknotes.'

components.note: 足 (foot) — 蹄 names the hoof, the animal equivalent of a foot.
帝 (dì) gives a sound close to tí, sharing the same rhyme and a related initial, differing in tone.

example.pinyin: Zhūtí shì yí dào yǒumíng de cài.
example.english: Pig's trotters is a famous dish.
example.fact: 蹄 names an animal's hoof, and 猪蹄 (zhūtí, pig's trotters) is a well-known dish in Chinese cuisine.

etymologyHint: A dog turned to the side

components.note: 犬 is a simplified picture of a dog seen from the side, with its head, back, and legs traced in a few strokes.

example.english: Police dogs are very smart.
example.fact: 犬 is the formal, written word for 'dog' — in everyday spoken Mandarin, people almost always say 狗 (gǒu) instead.

meanings: (literary) body (of a human, esp. the torso)
etymologyHint: To bow 弓 one's body 身; 弓 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 身 depicts a human body — 躬 refers to the body itself, or to bowing it.
弓 depicts a bow bent into a curve — that same curving shape suggests a body bent forward, giving 躬 its meaning 'to bow, to bend.'

example.english: He bowed to the teacher.
example.fact: 躬 rarely stands alone — it mainly appears in 鞠躬 (jūgōng), the word for the traditional bow used as a greeting or sign of respect.

etymologyHint: When the sun is a foot 尺 above the horizon 旦

components.note: 尺 depicts a ruler used to measure a foot's length, here used to mark off a distance.
旦 depicts the sun rising above the horizon line — placed a 'foot' below the measuring mark, the two together evoke daytime, giving 昼 its meaning 'daytime.'

example.english: The desert has a huge difference between day and night temperatures.
example.fact: 昼 is the literary word for 'daytime,' paired with 夜 (night) in 昼夜 (zhòuyè), 'day and night.'

components.note: 艹 (grass/plant) — 藻 names aquatic plants, algae.
澡 (zǎo) gives the sound — an exact match with 藻.

example.english: Seaweed can be eaten.
example.fact: 藻 names algae and seaweed — 海藻 (hǎizǎo) is a common ingredient in East Asian cooking.

components.note: 虫 (insect) — 蛛 names a small creature, the spider.
朱 (zhū) gives the sound — an exact match with 蛛.

example.english: The spider is weaving its web.
example.fact: 蛛 never stands alone — it only appears in 蜘蛛 (zhīzhū), the word for 'spider.'

components.note: 衤 (cloth) — 褐 originally named a coarse cloth, later coming to describe a brown color.
曷 (hé) gives a sound close to hè, the same syllable with a different tone.

example.pinyin: Zhè zhī xióng shì hèsè de.
example.english: This bear is brown.
example.fact: 褐 is the character for the color 'brown' in 褐色 (hèsè), as seen in animals like the brown bear (褐熊).

etymologyHint: The jaw in 夹 the head 页; 夹 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 夹 depicts something squeezed between two sides.
页 depicts a head — paired with the idea of being pinched between, the two together point to the sides of the face, giving 颊 its meaning 'cheek.'

example.english: The kitten's cheeks are very soft.
example.fact: 颊 almost always appears with 脸 as 脸颊 (liǎnjiá), the standard word for 'cheek.'

etymologyHint: A man 大 lifting up an offering of wine 酋

components.note: 酋 depicts a wine vessel with a lid, used in old ceremonies.
大 depicts a person standing with arms spread — placed under the vessel, the image is of someone lifting up an offering of wine, giving 奠 its meaning 'to offer in sacrifice, to establish.'

example.english: He laid the foundation.
example.fact: 奠 survives mainly in the compound 奠定 (diàndìng), meaning 'to lay a foundation' or 'to establish.'

components.note: 力 (strength) — 募 describes rallying effort or resources from others.
莫 (mò) gives a sound close to mù, sharing the same rhyme and initial, differing only in tone.

example.english: The school organizes a donation drive.
example.fact: 募 is the character behind 募捐 (mùjuān), 'to raise donations,' and 招募 (zhāomù), 'to recruit.'

components.note: 耳 (ear) — 耽's connection to the ear has faded; today it mostly describes delay or indulgence.
冘 (yín) gives a sound distantly related to dān, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: Don't waste time.
example.fact: 耽 is most common in 耽误 (dānwù), 'to delay' or 'hold up,' as in delaying someone's plans.

components.note: 足 (foot) — 蹈 describes stepping or treading, an action of the foot.
舀 (yǎo) gives a sound distantly related to dǎo, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: She likes learning dance.
example.fact: 蹈 mainly appears in 舞蹈 (wǔdǎo), the general word for 'dance.'

components.note: 阝 (hill/village) — 陋 originally described a rough, out-of-the-way village, extending to mean 'crude, humble.'

example.english: This house is very simple and crude.
example.fact: 陋 usually appears in 简陋 (jiǎnlòu), 'crude, simple,' or 丑陋 (chǒulòu), 'ugly.'

components.note: 亻 (person) — 侣 names a person who accompanies another.
吕 (lǚ) gives the sound — an exact match with 侣.

example.pinyin: Tāmen shì hěn hǎo de bànlǚ.
example.english: They are great partners.
example.fact: 侣 mostly appears in 伴侣 (bànlǚ), the common word for 'partner' or 'companion.'

etymologyHint: A forest 未 demon 鬼; 未 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 未 depicts a tree with young, unripe branches.
鬼 depicts a ghost or spirit with a strange, masked head — paired with the tree, it evokes something hidden deep in the woods, giving 魅 its meaning 'demon, enchanting.'

example.pinyin: Zhè zuò chéngshì hěn yǒu mèilì.
example.english: This city has a lot of charm.
example.fact: 魅 almost never stands alone — it's best known from 魅力 (mèilì), the common word for 'charm' or 'attraction.'

etymologyHint: Wind 风 blowing off the mountain 山

components.note: 山 depicts a mountain, three peaks in a row.
风 depicts wind — placed beneath the mountain, the two together evoke a mist stirred up by wind on a mountainside, giving 岚 its meaning 'mountain mist.'

example.pinyin: Shān shàng de lán hěn měi.
example.english: The mountain mist is very beautiful.
example.fact: 岚 is a literary word for the misty haze that gathers around mountains, and today survives mostly in place names and poetry.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 侄 names a family member, one's nephew.
至 (zhì) gives a sound close to zhí, the same syllable with a different tone.

example.english: This is my nephew.
example.fact: 侄 forms 侄子 (zhízi, 'nephew') and 侄女 (zhínǔ, 'niece'), naming the children of one's siblings.

etymologyHint: A tiger 虍 baring its claws 彐

components.note: 虍 depicts a tiger's head and stripes.
彐 depicts a claw or hand — placed with the tiger, the image is of bared claws, giving 虐 its meaning 'cruel, to abuse.'

example.english: You must not abuse animals.
example.fact: 虐 mainly appears in 虐待 (nüèdài), the standard word for 'to mistreat' or 'to abuse.'

components.note: 土 (earth) — 堕 describes falling down toward the ground.
陏 (Suí) gives a sound distantly related to duò, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: He gradually degenerated.
example.fact: 堕 is most common in 堕落 (duòluò), meaning 'to degenerate' or 'to fall into a bad state,' whether morally or literally.

components.note: 阝 (hill) — 陛 named the raised stairway leading up to a throne.
坒 (bì) gives the sound — an exact match with 陛.

example.english: People address the emperor as 'Your Majesty.'
example.fact: 陛 survives only in 陛下 (bìxià), the formal title 'Your Majesty,' literally referring to the steps below the throne.

etymologyHint: Simplified form of 瑩; fiery 火 like a gem 玉

components.note: 冖 depicts a cover — in the traditional form 瑩, this position held 火 (fire) twice, suggesting a fiery glow.
玉 depicts a piece of jade — combined with the glow above, the image is of a gem shining brightly, giving 莹 its meaning 'lustrous, bright as a gem.'

example.english: The dewdrop is very sparkling and clear.
example.fact: 莹 usually appears in 晶莹 (jīngyíng), a word describing something sparkling and crystal-clear, like dew or gems.

etymologyHint: Shade 阴 provided by a tree 艹; 阴 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 艹 depicts grass or plants, here standing for a tree providing shade.
阴 depicts shade, the shadowed side of a hill — paired with the plant above, the image is of shade cast by a tree, giving 荫 its meaning 'shade, shelter.'

example.pinyin: Xiàtiān, wǒmen zuò zài shùyīn xià.
example.english: In summer, we sit in the shade of a tree.
example.fact: 荫 is almost always paired with 树 as 树荫 (shùyīn), meaning 'the shade of a tree.'

components.note: 犭 (dog/animal) — 狡 groups cunning behavior with animal-related characters.
交 (jiāo) gives a sound close to jiǎo, the same syllable with a different tone.

example.english: The fox is very cunning.
example.fact: 狡 is best known from 狡猾 (jiǎohuá), 'cunning' or 'sly,' a trait often associated with foxes in Chinese stories.

components.note: 门 (gate) — 阀 originally referred to a family's gate or rank, later broadening to 'faction, powerful clique.'
伐 (fá) gives the sound — an exact match with 阀.

example.english: This valve is broken.
example.fact: 阀 has two very different modern uses: 军阀 (jūnfá, 'warlord') for a powerful faction, and 阀门 (fámén, 'valve') for the mechanical part.

components.note: 纟 (thread) — 绞 describes twisting strands together, like thread.
交 (jiāo) gives a sound close to jiǎo, the same syllable with a different tone.

example.english: Mom uses a meat grinder to grind meat.
example.fact: 绞 describes twisting or wringing something, as in 绞肉机 (jiǎoròujī), a 'meat grinder.'

components.note: ⺼ (flesh) — 膏 originally referred to animal fat, later extended to any thick paste.
高 (gāo) gives the sound — an exact match with 膏.

example.pinyin: Wǒ měitiān yòng yágāo shuā yá.
example.english: I brush my teeth with toothpaste every day.
example.fact: 膏 names a thick paste or ointment — 牙膏 (yágāo, 'toothpaste') is the most common everyday example.

components.note: 土 (earth) — 垮 describes something collapsing to the ground.
夸 (kuā) gives a sound close to kuǎ, the same syllable with a different tone.

example.pinyin: Tā tài lèi le, shēntǐ kuǎ le.
example.english: He was so tired his health collapsed.
example.fact: 垮 describes something collapsing or breaking down, whether a building, a plan, or a person's health, as in 累垮 (lèi kuǎ), 'worn out from exhaustion.'

components.note: 艹 (grass/plant) — 茎 names the stem or stalk of a plant.

example.pinyin: Zhè duǒ huā de jīng hěn cháng.
example.english: This flower's stem is very long.
example.fact: 茎 is the botanical word for a plant's 'stem' or 'stalk.'

components.note: 纟 (thread) — 缅's link to thread has faded; it now mostly means 'distant,' and appears in the name Myanmar.
面 (miàn) gives a sound close to miǎn, the same syllable with a different tone.

example.english: Myanmar is to the south of China.
example.fact: 缅 is most often seen in 缅甸 (Miǎndiàn), the Chinese name for Myanmar.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 喇 relates to a sound made with the mouth, as in a horn's blare.
剌 (là) gives a sound close to lǎ, the same syllable with a different tone.

example.english: The car's horn is very loud.
example.fact: 喇 only appears in 喇叭 (lǎba), the word for a 'horn' or 'loudspeaker.'

components.note: 纟 (silk/thread) — 绒 names a soft, fuzzy woven fabric.
戎 (róng) gives the sound — an exact match with 绒.

example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn máoyī shì yángróng de.
example.english: This sweater is made of cashmere.
example.fact: 绒 names soft fabrics like 羊绒 (yángróng, 'cashmere') and appears in 绒毛 (róngmáo), the word for soft, fine 'fluff' or 'down.'

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 搅 describes stirring something with the hands.
觉 (jiào) gives a sound close to jiǎo, the same syllable with a different tone.

example.english: Please stir the eggs a bit.
example.fact: 搅 is the verb in 搅拌 (jiǎobàn), 'to stir' or 'to mix,' a common step in cooking.

components.note: 几 (table/stool) — 凳 names a simple seat, a stool.
登 (dēng) gives a sound close to dèng, the same syllable with a different tone.

example.english: Please sit on the stool.
example.fact: 凳 names a simple backless seat — 凳子 (dèngzi) is the everyday word for 'stool.'

components.note: 木 (wood) — 梭 names a wooden tool used in weaving, the shuttle.
夋 (qūn) gives a sound distantly related to suō, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: Cars shuttle back and forth on the street.
example.fact: 梭 originally named the weaving shuttle, and survives today in 穿梭 (chuānsuō), 'to shuttle back and forth.'

components.note: 丫 is a simple picture of a line that splits into two branches at the top, like a fork in a road.

example.pinyin: Zhè gēn shùzhī de xíngzhuàng xiàng yā.
example.english: This branch's shape looks like a Y.
example.fact: 丫 pictures a forked shape, and today it's often used to describe a Y-shaped fork in a branch or road (树丫, shùyā).

etymologyHint: An official 臣 woman 女

components.note: 女 depicts a kneeling woman.
臣 depicts an official or servant kneeling before a ruler — paired with 女, it originally marked a woman of the court, giving 姬 its old meaning 'court lady.'

example.pinyin: Jī shì yí gè gǔdài de xìng.
example.english: Ji is an ancient surname.
example.fact: 姬 today survives mainly as a surname and in the names of historical figures and characters from Chinese mythology and legend.

etymologyHint: To issue 讠 a decree 召; 召 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 讠 depicts speech, a simplified form of 言.
召 depicts summoning someone with a call — paired with speech, the image is of an order spoken aloud, giving 诏 its meaning 'imperial edict.'

example.english: The emperor wrote an imperial edict.
example.fact: 诏 refers specifically to an emperor's official order, most often seen in the word 诏书 (zhàoshū), 'imperial edict.'

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 钮 names a small metal fastener, a button.
丑 (chǒu) gives a sound distantly related to niǔ, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: Please press this button.
example.fact: 钮 mainly appears in 按钮 (ànniǔ), the word for a mechanical or electronic 'button.'

components.note: 木 (wood) — 棺 names a wooden box used for burial, a coffin.
官 (guān) gives the sound — an exact match with 棺.

example.pinyin: Guāncai shì yòng mùtou zuò de.
example.english: Coffins are made of wood.
example.fact: 棺 forms 棺材 (guāncai), the everyday word for 'coffin.'

components.note: 火 (fire) — 耿 originally described the bright glow of a light, later extended to mean 'upright, honest.'

example.pinyin: Tā shì yí gè gěngzhí de rén.
example.english: He is a very forthright person.
example.fact: 耿 is best known from 耿直 (gěngzhí), a compliment describing someone who is honest and straightforward.

components.note: 纟 (thread) — 缔's original sense was tying a knot, extended to mean 'to conclude, to establish.'
帝 (dì) gives the sound — an exact match with 缔.

example.pinyin: Tā dìzàole yí gè xīn gōngsī.
example.english: He founded a new company.
example.fact: 缔 usually appears in formal words like 缔造 (dìzào), 'to found,' and 缔结 (dìjié), 'to conclude (an agreement).'

components.note: 忄 (heart) — 懈 describes a state of mind that has grown lazy or slack.
解 (xiè) gives the sound — an exact match with 懈.

example.hanzi: 他一直很努力，没有松懈。
example.pinyin: Tā yìzhí hěn nǔlì, méiyǒu sōngxiè.
example.english: He has always worked hard, without slacking off.
example.fact: 懈 mainly appears in 松懈 (sōngxiè), 'to slacken,' and 不懈 (bùxiè), describing effort that never lets up.

etymologyHint: An envious 疾 woman 女; 疾 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 女 depicts a kneeling woman.
疾 depicts someone struck by an arrow, an illness — paired with 女, it evokes a mind afflicted by envy, giving 嫉 its meaning 'jealous.'

example.hanzi: 他很嫉妒哥哥的新自行车。
example.pinyin: Tā hěn jídù gēge de xīn zìxíngchē.
example.english: He's very jealous of his older brother's new bicycle.
example.fact: 嫉 almost always appears in 嫉妒 (jídù), the everyday word for 'jealous, envious.'

etymologyHint: A clay 土 oven 火

components.note: 火 depicts flames.
土 depicts a mound of earth — paired with fire, the image is of a clay hearth built for cooking, giving 灶 its meaning 'kitchen stove.'

example.pinyin: Nǎinai zài zàotái qián zuò fàn.
example.english: Grandma is cooking in front of the stove.
example.fact: 灶 names the traditional wood or coal-fired stove once found in every Chinese kitchen, now mostly replaced by gas or electric stoves.

etymologyHint: Using a spoon 勹 to measure out two equal parts 冫

components.note: 勹 depicts a wrapping motion, like an arm curving around something.
冫 depicts two drops or dots — placed inside the wrap, the image is of something divided evenly into equal parts, giving 匀 its meaning 'even, uniform.'

example.english: These colors are very even.
example.fact: 匀 usually appears in 均匀 (jūnyún), the everyday word for 'even' or 'uniform,' as in evenly mixed colors or evenly spaced objects.

components.note: 冊 (book/document) — 嗣 originally referred to formally recording a line of succession.
司 (sī) gives a sound close to sì, the same syllable with a different tone.

example.english: The king had no heir.
example.fact: 嗣 is a literary word for 'heir' or 'descendant,' most often seen in historical writing as 子嗣 (zǐsì).

components.note: 鸟 (bird) — 鸽 names a type of bird, the pigeon or dove.
合 (gě) gives a sound close to gē, the same syllable with a different tone.

example.pinyin: Gōngyuán lǐ yǒu hěn duō gēzi.
example.english: There are many pigeons in the park.
example.fact: 鸽 forms 鸽子 (gēzi), and the white dove is an international symbol of peace.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 澡 describes washing the body with water.
喿 (zào) gives a sound close to zǎo, the same syllable with a different tone.

example.english: I take a bath every day.
example.fact: 澡 only appears in 洗澡 (xǐzǎo), the everyday word for 'to bathe' or 'to shower.'

meanings: to bore a hole; to chisel; to dig
etymologyHint: A drill 丵 making a hole 凵

components.note: 丵 depicts a drill or chisel, held upright with a decorated handle.
凵 depicts an open pit or container — paired with the drill, the image is of boring a hole into something, giving 凿 its meaning 'chisel, to bore.'

example.english: The worker uses a chisel to make a hole.
example.fact: 凿 names the chisel, the tool used to carve or bore holes into wood and stone.

components.note: 纟 (thread) — 纬 named the horizontal threads in weaving, later extended to lines of latitude.
韦 (wéi) gives a sound close to wěi, the same syllable with a different tone.

example.english: Beijing's latitude is relatively high.
example.fact: 纬 forms 纬度 (wěidù), 'latitude,' the geographic lines running east-west around the globe.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 沸 describes water bubbling up as it boils.
弗 (fú) shares the initial f- with fèi, though the rhyme has drifted apart over time.

example.english: The water is already boiling.
example.fact: 沸 is the character in 沸腾 (fèiténg), 'to boil,' and 沸点 (fèidiǎn), 'boiling point.'

components.note: 田 (farm/field) — 畴 names cultivated farmland.
寿 (shòu) gives a sound close to chóu, sharing the same rhyme.

example.hanzi: 音乐和数学是不同的范畴。
example.pinyin: Yīnyuè hé shùxué shì bùtóng de fànchóu.
example.english: Music and math are different categories.
example.fact: 畴 survives today mainly in 范畴 (fànchóu), the common word for 'category' or 'scope.'

etymologyHint: A knife 刀 sharp enough to draw blood 丶

components.note: 刀 depicts a single-edged knife.
丶 marks a single dot placed right on the blade's edge, pointing to the sharp part of the knife, giving 刃 its meaning 'blade, edge.'

example.pinyin: Zhè bǎ dāo de rèn hěn fēnglì.
example.english: This knife's blade is very sharp.
example.fact: 刃 specifically names the cutting edge of a blade, most often seen in the word 刀刃 (dāorèn), 'blade' or 'edge of a knife.'

components.note: 辶 (walk/movement) — 遏 describes stopping something in its path.
曷 (hé) gives a sound close to è, sharing the same rhyme.

example.english: We must curb pollution.
example.fact: 遏 is most common in 遏制 (èzhì), a formal word meaning 'to check' or 'curb' a negative trend.

etymologyHint: The happy 乐 light of a flame 火

components.note: 火 depicts flames.
乐 depicts joy or music — paired with fire, the image is of a bright, flickering light, giving 烁 its meaning 'shining, glittering.'

example.english: The stars twinkle in the night sky.
example.fact: 烁 almost always appears in 闪烁 (shǎnshuò), the word for the twinkling or flickering of stars and lights.

etymologyHint: To taste 口 an odor 臭; 臭 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 口 depicts a mouth.
臭 depicts a nose above a dog, evoking a strong smell — paired with the mouth, the two together point to sensing an odor, giving 嗅 its meaning 'to smell, to sniff.'

example.english: Dogs' sense of smell is very sharp.
example.fact: 嗅 mainly appears in 嗅觉 (xiùjué), the word for the 'sense of smell,' and is well known for how sharp it is in dogs.

meanings: denote a sound or sharp noise (gunfire etc)

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 叭 represents a sound made by the mouth or an instrument, like a horn's blare.
八 (bā) gives the sound — an exact match with 叭.

example.pinyin: Lǎba fāchū hěn dà de shēngyīn.
example.english: The horn makes a very loud sound.
example.fact: 叭 pairs with 喇 to form 喇叭 (lǎba), 'horn' or 'loudspeaker' — 叭 itself imitates the honking sound.

components.note: 灬 (fire) — 熬 describes cooking something slowly over a low flame.
敖 (áo) gives the sound — an exact match with 熬.

example.english: He stayed up late yesterday.
example.fact: 熬 originally meant slow-cooking over heat, but today it's best known from 熬夜 (áoyè), 'to stay up late.'

components.note: 目 (eye) — 瞥 describes a quick action of the eye, a glance.
敝 (bì) gives a sound distantly related to piē, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: I caught a glimpse of his smile.
example.fact: 瞥 describes a quick, fleeting glance, most often seen in 瞥见 (piējiàn), 'to catch a glimpse of.'

components.note: 骨 (bone) — 骸 names the bones of the body, the skeleton.
亥 (hài) gives a sound close to hái, the same syllable with a different tone.

example.hanzi: 考古学家发现了古代的骸骨。
example.pinyin: Kǎogǔ xuéjiā fāxiànle gǔdài de háigǔ.
example.english: Archaeologists discovered ancient skeletal remains.
example.fact: 骸 refers to skeletal remains, most often seen in 骸骨 (háigǔ), a word used in archaeology and forensic contexts.

components.note: 大 (big) — 奢 describes excess or extravagance, something beyond what is needed.
者 (zhě) gives a sound distantly related to shē, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: This bag is very extravagant.
example.fact: 奢 is the character in 奢侈 (shēchǐ), 'extravagant' or 'luxurious,' and 奢侈品 (shēchǐpǐn), 'luxury goods.'

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 拙 describes clumsy or unskilled work done by hand.
出 (chū) gives a sound close to zhuō, sharing a similar rhyme.

example.english: His movements are very clumsy.
example.fact: 拙 mainly appears in 笨拙 (bènzhuō), the common word for 'clumsy' or 'awkward.'

components.note: 木 (wood) — 栋 named the main wooden beam holding up a roof, and now works as a measure word for buildings.
东 (dōng) gives a sound close to dòng, the same syllable with a different tone.

example.english: This building is very tall.
example.fact: 栋 is a measure word used for buildings, as in 一栋楼 (yí dòng lóu), 'one building.'

components.note: 毛 (fur/hair) — 毯 names a woven covering made from fur or wool.
炎 (yán) gives a sound distantly related to tǎn, having drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Kètīng lǐ yǒu yí kuài dìtǎn.
example.english: There is a carpet in the living room.
example.fact: 毯 forms 地毯 (dìtǎn, 'carpet') and 毛毯 (máotǎn, 'wool blanket').

components.note: 木 (tree) — 桐 names a type of tree.
同 (tóng) gives the sound — an exact match with 桐.

example.english: Parasol trees are planted on both sides of the street.
example.fact: 桐 mainly appears in 梧桐 (wútóng), a tree commonly planted along streets in Chinese cities like Shanghai.

etymologyHint: Many small 少 stones 石; 少 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 石 depicts a rock or stone.
少 depicts a small quantity — paired with stone, the image is of many tiny pieces of rock, giving 砂 its meaning 'sand, grit.'

example.english: The sand by the sea is very fine.
example.fact: 砂 is closely related to and often interchangeable with the more common character 沙, both meaning 'sand.'

etymologyHint: A dog 犬 surrounded by weeds 艹, 廾

components.note: 艹 depicts grass or weeds.
犬 depicts a dog.
廾 depicts two hands raised — together, the picture is of a dog lost in a thick tangle of weeds, giving 莽 its meaning 'reckless, thick undergrowth.'

example.english: He does things very recklessly.
example.fact: 莽 usually appears in 鲁莽 (lǔmǎng), meaning 'rash' or 'reckless.'

components.note: 氵 (water) — 泻 describes water rushing or pouring down.
写 (xiě) gives a sound close to xiè, the same syllable with a different tone.

example.english: He had diarrhea yesterday.
example.fact: 泻 is most often seen in the medical word 腹泻 (fùxiè), 'diarrhea.'

components.note: 土 (earth) — 坪 names a flat, open piece of ground.
平 (píng) gives the sound — an exact match with 坪.

example.pinyin: Gōngyuán lǐ yǒu yí piàn cǎopíng.
example.english: There is a lawn in the park.
example.fact: 坪 most commonly appears in 草坪 (cǎopíng), the everyday word for 'lawn.'

components.note: 木 (wood) — 梳 names a wooden or plastic tool for the hair, a comb.
㐬 (liú) gives a sound distantly related to shū, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: She combs her hair with a comb.
example.fact: 梳 is both the noun 梳子 (shūzi, 'comb') and the verb 'to comb,' as in 梳头 (shūtóu), 'to comb one's hair.'

meanings: various species of pine and fir

components.note: 木 (tree) — 杉 names a type of coniferous tree, the fir or cedar.
彡 (shān) gives the sound — an exact match with 杉.

example.pinyin: Zhè zhāng zhuōzi shì shānmù zuò de.
example.english: This table is made of fir wood.
example.fact: 杉 names fir and cedar trees, and 杉木 (shānmù) is a common building and furniture material in China.

components.note: 日 (sun) — 晤's link to the sun has faded; today it just means 'to meet.'
吾 (wú) gives a sound close to wù, the same syllable with a different tone.

example.pinyin: Liǎng wèi lǎo péngyou huìwù le.
example.english: Two old friends met.
example.fact: 晤 is a formal word for 'to meet,' most often seen in 会晤 (huìwù), used for meetings between officials or leaders.

components.note: 禾 (grain) — 稚 originally described a late-ripening grain, extending to mean 'young, immature.'
隹 (zhuī) gives a sound distantly related to zhì, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: This idea is a bit naive.
example.fact: 稚 is most common in 幼稚 (yòuzhì), meaning 'childish' or 'naive.'

components.note: 艹 (plant) — 蔬 names edible plants, vegetables.
疏 (shū) gives the sound — an exact match with 蔬.

example.pinyin: Duō chī shūcài duì shēntǐ hǎo.
example.english: Eating more vegetables is good for your health.
example.fact: 蔬 forms 蔬菜 (shūcài), the everyday word for 'vegetables.'

etymologyHint: Insects 虫 that toads 黾 feed on

components.note: 虫 depicts an insect.
黾 depicts a toad or frog with a round body — paired with the insect, it points to a small flying pest that toads like to eat, giving 蝇 its meaning 'fly.'

example.pinyin: Chúfáng lǐ yǒu yì zhī cāngyíng.
example.english: There is a fly in the kitchen.
example.fact: 蝇 almost always appears in 苍蝇 (cāngyíng), the everyday word for the common housefly.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 捣 describes pounding or striking something with the hands.
岛 (dǎo) gives the sound — an exact match with 捣.

example.english: My little brother always makes trouble.
example.fact: 捣 is best known from 捣乱 (dǎoluàn), the everyday phrase for 'to make trouble' or 'to cause a disturbance.'

meanings: a measure of area equal to 100 mu or 6.7 hectares

example.english: One qing of land is very large.
example.fact: 顷 is a traditional unit of land area, equal to 100 mu (about 6.7 hectares) — still used today when discussing farmland size in China.

components.note: 么 (tiny, insignificant) — 麽 shares this sense of smallness with 么, of which it is the traditional form.
麻 (má) gives a sound close to mó, the same syllable with a different tone.

example.english: What do you want?
example.fact: 麽 is a traditional variant of 么, most familiar from 甚麽/什麼, the older written form of 什么 (shénme), 'what.'

meanings: used in 尷尬|尴尬[gan1 ga4]

components.note: 尢 (lame/crooked leg) — 尴 groups awkwardness with this radical, suggesting an unsteady, uncomfortable position.
监 (jiān) gives a sound close to gān, sharing the same rhyme.

example.english: This situation is very awkward.
example.fact: 尴 never appears alone — it only exists in 尴尬 (gāngà), the everyday word for 'awkward' or 'embarrassing.'

meanings: goods sent under the protection of an armed escort

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 镖 names a small metal throwing weapon, a dart.
票 (piào) gives a sound close to biāo, sharing the same rhyme.

example.english: They are playing darts.
example.fact: 镖 today is best known from 飞镖 (fēibiāo), which names both the traditional throwing dart and the modern game of darts.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 诧 describes a reaction expressed through speech or expression, surprise.
宅 (zhái) gives a sound distantly related to chà, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: He looked at me in astonishment.
example.fact: 诧 mainly appears in 诧异 (chàyì), a formal word for 'astonished' or 'surprised.'

components.note: 尢 (lame/crooked leg) — like 尴, 尬 groups awkwardness with this radical of an unsteady stance.
介 (jiè) gives a sound distantly related to gà, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: He felt very embarrassed.
example.fact: 尬 only exists as the second half of 尴尬 (gāngà), 'awkward' or 'embarrassing' — it has no independent use.

components.note: 石 (mineral/stone) — 硫 names a mineral element, sulfur.
㐬 (liú) gives the sound — an exact match with 硫.

example.pinyin: Liú shì yì zhǒng huàxué yuánsù.
example.english: Sulfur is a chemical element.
example.fact: 硫 (sulfur) is best known for its strong smell, similar to the smell often associated with volcanoes.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 嚼 describes chewing, an action of the mouth.
爵 (jué) gives the sound — an exact match with 嚼.

example.english: You should chew slowly when eating.
example.fact: 嚼 is the everyday verb for 'to chew,' often paired with 咀 as 咀嚼 (jǔjué).

etymologyHint: Someone who has a whole row 次 of sheep 羊

components.note: 羊 depicts a sheep.
次 depicts saliva dripping from an open mouth — paired with the sheep, the image is of someone drooling over a flock of sheep, giving 羡 its meaning 'to envy, admire.'

example.pinyin: Wǒ hěn xiànmù nǐ de fángzi.
example.english: I really admire your house.
example.fact: 羡 is almost always used in the word 羡慕 (xiànmù), the common word for 'to envy' or 'to admire.'

components.note: 氵 (water) — 沦 describes sinking down into water, extended to mean 'to fall into ruin.'
仑 (lún) gives the sound — an exact match with 沦.

example.pinyin: Tā de shēnghuó jiànjiàn lúnluò le.
example.english: His life gradually fell into ruin.
example.fact: 沦 is most common in 沦落 (lúnluò) and 沦为 (lúnwéi), both describing a decline into a worse state.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 沪 originally named a river-fishing device, and became a short name for the city built beside it, Shanghai.
户 (hù) gives the sound — an exact match with 沪.

example.english: Hù is the short name for Shanghai.
example.fact: 沪 is the one-character abbreviation for Shanghai, seen on license plates and in names like 沪剧 (hùjù), Shanghai opera.

etymologyHint: A wide 广 plain under the sun 日; 广 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 日 depicts the sun.
广 depicts a lean-to shelter, open on one side — paired with the sun, the image is of an open, sunlit space, giving 旷 its meaning 'vast, empty.'

example.english: He skipped class today.
example.fact: 旷 shows up in student life mainly through 旷课 (kuàngkè), meaning 'to skip class without permission.'

components.note: 彡 (hair/fine lines) — 彬 uses decorative strokes to suggest refinement and polish.
林 (lín) gives a sound close to bīn, sharing the same rhyme.

example.english: He speaks in a refined and courteous way.
example.fact: 彬 is best known from 彬彬有礼 (bīnbīn yǒulǐ), a phrase praising someone's polished, courteous manner.

components.note: 艹 (plant) — 芽 names the first shoot a plant sends up, a bud.
牙 (yá) gives the sound — an exact match with 芽.

example.english: In spring, the seeds sprout.
example.fact: 芽 is the character for a plant's 'sprout' or 'bud,' as in 豆芽 (dòuyá), 'bean sprouts.'

meanings: (bound form) used in the names of small mammals

components.note: 犭 (animal) — 狸 names a small mammal, grouped with other animal characters.
里 (lǐ) gives a sound close to lí, the same syllable with a different tone.

example.english: Foxes are very clever.
example.fact: 狸 mainly appears in 狐狸 (húli), the everyday word for 'fox.'

etymologyHint: The sun 日, covered 冖, with 六 providing the pronunciation

components.note: 冖 depicts a cover.
日 depicts the sun.
六 here does not mean 'six' — it depicts two open hands, once used to show the sun being covered and hidden, giving 冥 its meaning 'dark, deep.'

example.english: He meditates for ten minutes every day.
example.fact: 冥 today is best known from 冥想 (míngxiǎng), the modern word for 'meditation.'

components.note: 石 (mineral/stone) — 碳 names a chemical element, carbon.
炭 (tàn) gives the sound — an exact match with 碳.

example.english: Plants need carbon dioxide.
example.fact: 碳 (carbon) is the basic element of all known life, and appears in everyday science terms like 二氧化碳 (èryǎnghuàtàn), 'carbon dioxide.'

meanings: used in 大大咧咧[da4 da4 lie1 lie1]
used in 罵罵咧咧|骂骂咧咧[ma4 ma5 lie1 lie1]

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 咧 describes stretching the mouth wide, as in a grin.
列 (liè) gives a sound close to liě, the same syllable with a different tone.

example.english: He grinned widely.
example.fact: 咧 describes the mouth stretching into a wide grin, most often seen in 咧嘴 (liězuǐ).

components.note: 忄 (heart) — 惕 describes a wary, alert state of mind.
易 (yì) gives a sound distantly related to tì, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: We must stay vigilant.
example.fact: 惕 only appears in 警惕 (jǐngtì), the common word for 'to be on guard' or 'vigilant.'

components.note: 日 (sun) — 暑 describes the hot weather brought by the summer sun.
者 (zhě) gives a sound distantly related to shǔ, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: I'm going to travel during summer vacation.
example.fact: 暑 forms 暑假 (shǔjià), the everyday word for 'summer vacation.'

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 咯 marks a sound made with the mouth, whether a cough or a spoken particle.
各 (gè) gives a sound close to gē, the same syllable with a different tone.

example.english: Okay then, let's go.
example.fact: 咯 is a casual sentence-final particle, similar to 了 or 啦, often adding a light, relaxed tone to a sentence.

components.note: 艹 (plant) — 萝 names a creeping vine or root vegetable.
罗 (luó) gives the sound — an exact match with 萝.

example.english: Rabbits like to eat carrots.
example.fact: 萝 forms 胡萝卜 (húluóbo, 'carrot') and 萝卜 (luóbo, 'radish'), two very common vegetables in Chinese cooking.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 汹 describes turbulent, surging water.
凶 (xiōng) gives the sound — an exact match with 汹.

example.english: The sea waves are surging.
example.fact: 汹 almost always appears in 汹涌 (xiōngyǒng), describing violently churning water, like turbulent ocean waves.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh/meat) — 腥 describes the strong smell of raw meat or fish.
星 (xīng) gives the sound — an exact match with 腥.

example.english: This fish has a fishy smell.
example.fact: 腥 describes the strong, raw smell of fish or meat, most often seen in 腥味 (xīngwèi), 'fishy smell.'

components.note: 穴 (hole/cave) — 窥 describes peeking through a small opening.
规 (guī) gives a sound close to kuī, sharing the same rhyme.

example.english: He secretly peeked into the room.
example.fact: 窥 describes secretly peeking or spying, most often seen in 窥视 (kuīshì) and 偷窥 (tōukuī), 'to peep.'

components.note: 亻 (person) — 俺 is a personal pronoun, referring to a person: 'I, me.'
奄 (yǎn) gives a sound close to ǎn, sharing the same rhyme.

example.english: I am a farmer.
example.fact: 俺 is a dialectal word for 'I' or 'me,' common in Northern Chinese regions, used instead of the standard 我 (wǒ).

components.note: 氵 (water) — 潭 names a deep pool of water.
覃 (Qín) gives a sound distantly related to tán, having drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Shān lǐ yǒu yí gè shēntán.
example.english: There is a deep pool in the mountains.
example.fact: 潭 names a deep pool of water, and appears in many place names across China, like 日月潭 (Rìyuè Tán), 'Sun Moon Lake' in Taiwan.

components.note: 山 (mountain) — 崎 describes rugged, uneven mountain terrain.
奇 (qí) gives the sound — an exact match with 崎.

example.pinyin: Zhè tiáo shān lù hěn qíqū.
example.english: This mountain road is very rugged.
example.fact: 崎 only appears in 崎岖 (qíqū), the word for rugged, bumpy terrain.

components.note: 鹿 (deer) — 麟 names a legendary, deer-like creature, the Chinese unicorn.
粦 (lín) gives the sound — an exact match with 麟.

example.hanzi: 麒麟是中国传说中的动物。
example.pinyin: Qílín shì Zhōngguó chuánshuō zhōng de dòngwù.
example.english: The qilin is an animal from Chinese legend.
example.fact: 麟 forms 麒麟 (qílín), a mythical hoofed creature in Chinese folklore, often seen as a symbol of good fortune.

meanings: to pick up; to collect; to gather

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 捡 describes picking something up with the hand.
佥 (qiān) gives a sound close to jiǎn, sharing the same rhyme.

example.english: He found (picked up) 100 yuan.
example.fact: 捡 is the everyday verb for 'to pick up' something off the ground, as in 捡垃圾 (jiǎn lājī), 'to pick up trash.'

etymologyHint: To give 丞 a hand 扌; 丞 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 扌 depicts a hand.
丞 depicts two hands lifting someone out of a pit — paired with another hand, the image is of rescuing someone, giving 拯 its meaning 'to rescue, to save.'

example.hanzi: 消防员拯救了那只小狗。
example.pinyin: Xiāofángyuán zhěngjiùle nà zhī xiǎo gǒu.
example.english: The firefighter rescued that little dog.
example.fact: 拯 almost always appears in 拯救 (zhěngjiù), the common word for 'to rescue' or 'to save.'

components.note: 欮 (jué) gives the sound — an exact match with 厥. 厥's own meanings ('he, it'; 'to faint') developed separately from this sound-bearing part.

example.english: He suddenly fainted.
example.fact: 厥 today mostly appears in the medical word 昏厥 (hūnjué), 'to faint' or 'to lose consciousness.'

meanings: purify water by allowing sediment to settle

components.note: 氵 (water) — 澄 describes water becoming clear once sediment settles.
登 (dēng) gives a sound distantly related to chéng, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: He clarified this misunderstanding.
example.fact: 澄 is best known from 澄清 (chéngqīng), meaning 'to clarify' a fact or 'to become clear,' like settled water.

components.note: 艹 (plant) — 萎 describes a plant wilting or withering.
委 (wěi) gives a sound close to wēi, the same syllable with a different tone.

example.english: The flower has withered.
example.fact: 萎 pairs with 枯 as 枯萎 (kūwěi), describing a plant that has withered and dried up.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 哉 marks an exclamation spoken aloud, like 'oh!' or 'how...!'

example.english: Alas! How sorrowful!
example.fact: 哉 is a classical exclamatory particle, similar to 'oh!' or 'how...!' in English — it survives today mainly in the set phrase 呜呼哀哉 (wūhū āi zāi), 'alas!'

etymologyHint: A mouth 呙 made of water 氵

components.note: 氵 depicts flowing water.
呙 depicts a crooked, twisting mouth — paired with water, the image is of water spinning around itself, giving 涡 its meaning 'whirlpool, eddy.'

example.pinyin: Hé lǐ yǒu yí gè xiǎo xuánwō.
example.english: There's a small whirlpool in the river.
example.fact: 涡 mostly appears in 漩涡 (xuánwō), the word for a 'whirlpool' or 'eddy' in flowing water.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 滔 describes water surging or overflowing.
舀 (yǎo) gives a sound distantly related to tāo, having drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Tā tāotāo bù jué de shuōhuà.
example.english: He talks on and on without stopping.
example.fact: 滔 is best known from 滔滔不绝 (tāotāo bù jué), a vivid phrase for someone who talks endlessly, like a river that never stops flowing.

components.note: 日 (sun) — 暇's link to the sun has faded; today it just means 'free time, leisure.'
叚 (jiǎ) gives a sound close to xiá, sharing the same rhyme.

example.english: I have free time on weekends.
example.fact: 暇 mainly appears in 闲暇 (xiánxiá), 'free time,' and 无暇 (wúxiá), 'to have no time to spare.'

etymologyHint: To seek the source 朔 of a river 氵

components.note: 氵 depicts flowing water.
朔 depicts the new moon, the start of the lunar month — paired with water, the image is of tracing a river back to its beginning, giving 溯 its meaning 'to go upstream, to trace back.'

example.hanzi: 这个传统可以追溯到很久以前。
example.pinyin: Zhège chuántǒng kěyǐ zhuīsù dào hěn jiǔ yǐqián.
example.english: This tradition can be traced back a very long time.
example.fact: 溯 almost always appears in 追溯 (zhuīsù), the word for 'to trace back' to an origin in time.

components.note: 鱼 (fish) — 鳞 names the scales covering a fish's body.
粦 (lín) gives the sound — an exact match with 鳞.

example.pinyin: Yú shēn shàng yǒu hěn duō lín.
example.english: There are many scales on the fish's body.
example.fact: 鳞 names the small, overlapping scales found on fish and snakes.

components.note: 酉 (wine vessel) — 酿 describes the process of fermenting, brewing wine or other drinks.
良 (liáng) gives a sound close to niàng, sharing the same rhyme.

example.english: This factory brews alcohol.
example.fact: 酿 is the verb for 'to brew' or 'to ferment,' as in 酿酒 (niàngjiǔ), 'to make wine or liquor.'

components.note: 艹 (grass) — 茵 names a soft mat or cushion, once made from woven grass.
因 (yīn) gives the sound — an exact match with 茵.

example.pinyin: Gōngyuán lǐ lǜ cǎo rú yīn.
example.english: The park's grass is lush and green, like a carpet.
example.fact: 茵 mainly survives in the idiom 绿草如茵 (lǜ cǎo rú yīn), describing grass so lush and even it looks like a green carpet.

components.note: 忄 (heart) — 愕 describes a sudden emotional reaction, shock.
咢 (è) gives the sound — an exact match with 愕.

example.hanzi: 听到这个消息，他很惊愕。
example.pinyin: Tīngdào zhège xiāoxi, tā hěn jīng'è.
example.english: Hearing this news, he was very astounded.
example.fact: 愕 usually appears in 惊愕 (jīng'è), a formal word for 'astounded' or 'stunned.'

components.note: 目 (eye) — 瞅 describes an action of the eye, to look or glance.
秋 (qiū) gives a sound close to chǒu, sharing a similar rhyme.

example.english: He glanced at me.
example.fact: 瞅 is a colloquial, mostly Northern Chinese word for 'to look' or 'to glance at,' similar to 看 (kàn).

components.note: 日 (sun) — 暮 describes the sun sinking low, marking the end of the day.
莫 (mò) gives a sound close to mù, sharing the same rhyme and initial, differing in tone.

example.english: Dusk has fallen.
example.fact: 暮 is a literary word for 'dusk' or 'evening,' as in 暮色 (mùsè), 'the light of dusk.'

components.note: 行 (to go/road) — 衙's link to movement has faded; it now names a government office.
吾 (wú) gives a sound distantly related to yá, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 古代的官员在衙门办公。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài de guānyuán zài yámén bàngōng.
example.english: Ancient officials worked in the yamen (government office).
example.fact: 衙 forms 衙门 (yámén), the historical term for a local government office in imperial China.

etymologyHint: Words 讠 of warning 戒; 戒 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 讠 depicts speech.
戒 depicts two hands holding a weapon on guard — paired with speech, the image is of a spoken warning, giving 诫 its meaning 'to admonish, warning.'

example.pinyin: Māma gàojiè wǒ bú yào shuōhuǎng.
example.english: Mom warned me not to lie.
example.fact: 诫 almost always appears in 告诫 (gàojiè), a formal word for 'to warn' or 'to admonish.'

components.note: 斤 (axe) — 斧 names a heavier, two-handed cutting tool, the axe.
父 (fù) gives a sound close to fǔ, the same syllable with a different tone.

example.english: He chops the tree with an axe.
example.fact: 斧 names the axe, a tool for chopping wood, as in 斧头 (fǔtou).

meanings: (particle in old Chinese similar to 啊)

example.english: The road is long, oh, and far-reaching.
example.fact: 兮 is a classical Chinese particle, roughly like a dramatic 'oh!' or 'ah!' in English — it appears throughout ancient poetry (like Qu Yuan's Li Sao) but not in modern spoken Mandarin.

components.note: 火 (fire) — 焕 describes a bright, radiant glow.
奂 (huàn) gives the sound — an exact match with 焕.

example.english: She looks radiant and full of energy today.
example.fact: 焕 is best known from 精神焕发 (jīngshén huànfā), a phrase describing someone looking radiant and full of energy.

components.note: 木 (tree) — 棕 names the palm tree, and the brown color associated with its fiber.
宗 (zōng) gives the sound — an exact match with 棕.

example.pinyin: Zhè zhī xióng shì zōngsè de.
example.english: This bear is brown.
example.fact: 棕 names the color 'brown' in 棕色 (zōngsè), and also the palm tree in 棕树 (zōngshù).

components.note: 亻 (person) — 佑 describes one person helping or protecting another.
右 (yòu) gives the sound — an exact match with 佑.

example.english: Mom hopes the gods will protect us.
example.fact: 佑 almost always appears in 保佑 (bǎoyòu), a word used when asking for divine protection or blessing.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 嘶 describes a rough sound made with the mouth or voice.
斯 (sī) gives the sound — an exact match with 嘶.

example.english: His voice is very hoarse.
example.fact: 嘶 describes a rough, hoarse sound — 嘶哑 (sīyǎ) is the common word for a 'hoarse' voice, and 马嘶 describes a horse's neigh.

etymologyHint: A working 支 woman 女; 支 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 女 depicts a kneeling woman.
支 depicts a hand holding a branch, suggesting work or a trade — paired with 女, it originally marked a woman working as an entertainer, giving 妓 its meaning 'prostitute.'

example.hanzi: 妓女是一个正式的书面词。
example.pinyin: Jìnǚ shì yí gè zhèngshì de shūmiàn cí.
example.english: 'Jìnǚ' is a formal, written word.
example.fact: 妓 only appears in the compound 妓女 (jìnǚ); it does not stand alone in modern spoken Mandarin.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 喧 describes loud talking or noise made with the mouth.
宣 (xuān) gives the sound — an exact match with 喧.

example.english: The street is very noisy.
example.fact: 喧 pairs with 闹 as 喧闹 (xuānnào), the common word for a loud, bustling 'noise.'

meanings: short name for Chengdu 成都[Cheng2 du1]
paste made by mashing beans or seeds etc
used in 芙蓉[fu2 rong2], lotus

components.note: 艹 (flower) — 蓉 names a flowering plant, the hibiscus/lotus.
容 (róng) gives the sound — an exact match with 蓉.

example.english: Chengdu is also called 'Hibiscus City.'
example.fact: 蓉 gives Chengdu its poetic nickname, 蓉城 (Róngchéng), 'Hibiscus City,' and its car license-plate abbreviation 蓉.

etymologyHint: To cut 刂 out passages from a book 册

components.note: 册 depicts a bound stack of bamboo strips, an early form of a book.
刂 depicts a knife — paired with the book, the image is of cutting passages out of a text, giving 删 its meaning 'to delete, to cut out.'

example.english: Please delete this photo.
example.fact: 删 is the everyday word for deleting text or files — most often seen in 删除 (shānchú), 'to delete.'

components.note: 木 (tree) — 樱 names a flowering tree, the cherry.
婴 (yīng) gives the sound — an exact match with 樱.

example.english: In spring, the cherry blossoms bloom.
example.fact: 樱 forms 樱花 (yīnghuā), 'cherry blossom,' famous for blooming across Japan and China every spring.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 伺 describes one person watching or attending to another.
司 (sī) gives a sound close to cì, sharing the same rhyme.

example.english: She takes care of the elderly every day.
example.fact: 伺 mainly appears in 伺候 (cìhou), meaning 'to wait upon' or 'attend to' someone's needs.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 嗡 imitates a sound, like the buzz of an insect.
翁 (wēng) gives the sound — an exact match with 嗡.

example.english: Bees fly around buzzing.
example.fact: 嗡 imitates the buzzing sound of bees, flies, and airplane engines, as in 嗡嗡 (wēngwēng).

components.note: 女 (woman) — 娥 describes a beautiful woman.
我 (wǒ) gives a sound distantly related to é, having drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Cháng'é shì yuèliang shàng de nǚshén.
example.english: Chang'e is the goddess on the moon.
example.fact: 娥 is best known from 嫦娥 (Cháng'é), the goddess of the moon in Chinese mythology, also the name of China's lunar exploration program.

meanings: pointed tip of something long like a branch

components.note: 木 (tree) — 梢 names the thin tip of a tree branch.
肖 (xiào) gives a sound distantly related to shāo, having drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Niǎo zài shùshāo shàng chàng gē.
example.english: The bird sings at the top of the tree.
example.fact: 梢 names the thin tip of a branch, most often seen in 树梢 (shùshāo), 'treetop.'

components.note: 土 (earth) — 坝 names an earthen structure built to hold back water, a dam.
贝 (bèi) gives a sound distantly related to bà, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: The Three Gorges Dam is very big.
example.fact: 坝 names a 'dam,' as in 三峡大坝 (Sānxiá Dàbà), the Three Gorges Dam, one of the largest dams in the world.

components.note: 虫 (insect) — 蚕 names an insect, the silkworm.
天 (tiān) gives a sound distantly related to cán, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: The farmer is raising silkworms.
example.fact: 蚕 (silkworm) produces the silk thread that gave China's ancient Silk Road its name.

components.note: 攵 (tap/strike) — 敷's link to striking has faded; it now describes spreading or applying something.
旉 (fū) gives the sound — an exact match with 敷.

example.english: She applies a face mask every day.
example.fact: 敷 is the verb for 'to apply' something to the skin, as in 敷面膜 (fū miànmó), 'to apply a face mask.'

components.note: 氵 (water) — 澜 describes big waves on open water.
阑 (lán) gives the sound — an exact match with 澜.

example.english: The sea's waves are grand and magnificent.
example.fact: 澜 mainly appears in 波澜 (bōlán), describing large waves — often used figuratively for dramatic ups and downs in life or history.

etymologyHint: A open mouth 口, waiting for fruit to fall from the tree 木

components.note: 木 depicts a tree.
口 depicts an open mouth — placed beneath the tree, the image is of a mouth waiting for fruit to drop, giving 杏 its meaning 'apricot.'

example.english: I like eating apricots.
example.fact: 杏 names the apricot, a fruit similar to a small peach, often dried and eaten as a snack in China.

components.note: 纟 (thread/silk) — 绥's link to thread has faded; it now means 'to pacify, calm.'
妥 (tuǒ) gives a sound distantly related to suí, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 绥化是黑龙江的一个城市。
example.pinyin: Suíhuà shì Hēilóngjiāng de yí gè chéngshì.
example.english: Suihua is a city in Heilongjiang.
example.fact: 绥 appears mainly in place names in Northeast China, like 绥化 (Suíhuà) and 绥远 (Suíyuǎn), an old province name.

example.english: Workers smelt metal.
example.fact: 冶 almost always appears in words like 冶炼 (yěliàn, 'to smelt') or 冶金 (yějīn, 'metallurgy'), describing the process of melting and refining metal.

components.note: 广 (house/shelter) — 庇 describes sheltering someone under a roof.
比 (bǐ) gives a sound close to bì, the same syllable with a different tone.

example.pinyin: Dà shù wéi wǒmen tígōng bìhù.
example.english: The big tree gives us shelter.
example.fact: 庇 usually appears in 庇护 (bìhù), the formal word for 'to shelter' or 'to protect.'

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 挠 describes scratching with the hand.
尧 (yáo) gives a sound close to náo, sharing the same rhyme.

example.english: He scratched his head.
example.fact: 挠 is the everyday verb for 'to scratch,' as in 挠头 (náo tóu), 'to scratch one's head,' often when puzzled.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 搂 describes pulling something close with the arms, a hug.
娄 (lóu) gives a sound close to lǒu, the same syllable with a different tone.

example.english: Mom hugs the child.
example.fact: 搂 is a common verb for 'to hug' or 'to hold close' with one's arms.

components.note: 犬 (dog) — 倏's link to the dog radical is mostly historical; the character today only means 'suddenly.'
攸 (yōu) gives a sound distantly related to shū, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: Time passes by in an instant.
example.fact: 倏 is a literary word for 'suddenly,' most often seen in 倏忽 (shūhū), describing something happening in a flash.

etymologyHint: A pair 双 of ears 耳

components.note: 耳 depicts an ear.
双 depicts a pair of hands together, marking 'two' — paired with the ear, the image is of two ears close together, as if whispering, giving 聂 its meaning 'to whisper.'

example.pinyin: Niè shì Zhōngguó rén de yí gè xìng.
example.english: Nie is a Chinese surname.
example.fact: 聂 today is used almost only as a surname; its old meaning 'to whisper' is rarely used.

components.note: 女 (woman) — 婉 describes a gentle, graceful manner.
宛 (wǎn) gives the sound — an exact match with 婉.

example.english: He tactfully declined.
example.fact: 婉 is best known from 委婉 (wěiwǎn), describing a tactful, indirect way of saying something, often to soften bad news.

meanings: (bound form) to make a cacophonous noise
etymologyHint: The sound 口 of birds chirping 喿; 喿 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 口 depicts a mouth.
喿 depicts three mouths in a tree, representing birds chirping — paired with another mouth, the image is one of noisy chatter, giving 噪 its meaning 'noisy.'

example.english: The noise outside is very loud.
example.fact: 噪 almost always appears in 噪音 (zàoyīn), the everyday word for unwanted 'noise.'

components.note: 禾 (grain) — 稼 describes planting and growing crops.
家 (jiā) gives a sound close to jià, the same syllable with a different tone.

example.pinyin: Nóngmín zài tián lǐ zhòng zhuāngjia.
example.english: Farmers grow crops in the fields.
example.fact: 稼 forms 庄稼 (zhuāngjia), the everyday word for farm 'crops.'
